o: Jonah, sent to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish.
He is stayed by a tempest.
He is cast into the sea, and miraculously preserved.
bg: jonah, book of
This book professes to give an account of what actually took place in the experience of the prophet. Some critics have sought to interpret the book as a parable or allegory, and not as a history.
Tarshish

Probably Tartessus, a city and emporium of the Phoenicians in the south of Spain, represented as one of the sons of Javan. (Genesis 10:4; 1 Kings 10:22; 1 Chronicles 1:7; Psalms 48:7; Isaiah 2:16; Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12,25; Jonah 1:3; 4:2) The identity of the two places is rendered highly probable by the following circumstances: 1st.
Nineveh

First mentioned in Gen. 10:11, which is rendered in the Revised Version, "He [i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria and builded Nineveh." It is not again noticed till the days of Jonah, when it is described (Jonah 3:3; 4:11) as a great and populous city, the flourishing capital of the Assyrian empire (2 Kings 19:36; Isa. 37:37).
Joppa

Beauty, a town in the portion of Dan (Josh. 19:46; A.V., "Japho"), on a sandy promontory between Caesarea and Gaza, and at a distance of 30 miles north-west from Jerusalem. It is one of the oldest towns in Asia.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Jonah, sent to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish (vv. 1–3); He is stayed by a tempest (vv. 4–7); His discourse with the mariners (vv. 8–12); He is cast into the sea, and miraculously preserved (vv. 13–17). People named: Jonah, Amittai. Places: Tarshish, Nineveh, Joppa.
ch.mh: It is sad to think how much sin is committed in great cities.
q: Read verses 1–3 (Jonah, sent to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 4–7 (He is stayed by a tempest), what do you learn about prayer?
Verse 1 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Luke 11:32. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jonah’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Jonah?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us see this salvation of the Lord, and admire his power, that he could thus save a drowning man, and his pity, that he would thus save one who was running from him, and had offended him.
ch.a: Set aside a specific time this week to pray through this chapter's key verse.

o: He is delivered from the fish.
bg: jonah, book of
This book professes to give an account of what actually took place in the experience of the prophet. Some critics have sought to interpret the book as a parable or allegory, and not as a history.
Jonah

(dove), the fifth of the minor prophets, was the son of Amittai, and a native of Gath-hepher. (2 Kings 14:25) He flourished in or before the reign of Jeroboam II., about B.C. 820. Having already, as it seems, prophesied to Israel, he was sent to Nineveh.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The prayer of Jonah (vv. 1–9); He is delivered from the fish (vv. 10). People named: Jonah.
q: Read verses 1–9 (The prayer of Jonah). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 10 (He is delivered from the fish), what do you learn about prayer?
Verse 2 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Psalms 18:4–6. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jonah’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of salvation and redemption in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Jonah?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us confess our sins, consider Christ's resurrection as an earnest of our own, and thankfully receive every temporal and spiritual deliverance, as the pledge of our eternal redemption.
ch.a: Set aside a specific time this week to pray through this chapter's key verse.

In verses 5–10 (Nineveh is spared upon the repentance of the inhabitants), what do you learn about sin and repentance?

ch.aq: Let us boldly cast ourselves down at the footstool of free grace, and God will look upon us with compassion.

He is taught by the withering of a gourd, that he did wrong.

In verses 5–11 (He is taught by the withering of a gourd, that he did wrong), what do you learn about grace and mercy?
Verse 2 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Psalms 86:15. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jonah’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Jonah?

ch.aq: Let us study our own hearts and ways; let us not forget our own ingratitude and obstinacy; and let us be astonished at God's patience towards us.
ch.a: Show the same mercy you have received to someone who does not deserve it.
